SubDecay browse by type volume/amplification amplification preamp / clean boost browse by enclosure pedal SubDecay Vector - Analog Preamp Published on November 12, 2017 SubDecay boost / preamp pedal Information SubDecay Vector Overview Sometimes you just want to get things done. Hauling multiple amps around isnâ€™t fun. Tearing up your pedalboard to record a fleeting inspiration just slows you down. Enter the Vector Analog Preamp. Itâ€™s like eleven pedals in one, but without all the gimmicky features that often make â€œmultiâ€ pedals difficult to use. The Vector uses digital technology to control multiple gain stages and a full internal tone stack. This gives you unmatched tonal variation with easy to use familiar controls, Volume, Tone and Gain. The Vector wonâ€™t get in the way or eat up half of your pedalboard. Overdrive, distortion and Fuzz! Oh my! The Vector covers all your fuzz and drive needs with eleven channels of dirty analog goodness. Even with all the options you still get the simple control surface you expect in a stompbox. The tones. The tones. The TOANZ! None of the channels are clones or â€œmodels,â€ but they do all have their own inspirations. Drive 1 & 2 Similar to that well known green overdrive, but without the tubby cleanish signal underneath. This makes the drive 1 & 2 channels more useful when with a clean amp, but will still push a dirty amp into a screaming sustain machine. Drive 2 is similar, but with more bass response and a less prominent midrange hump. Crunch The crunch channelâ€™s tight bass response and harmonic clarity make it perfect for palm muting and general purpose riff rock. Do you think youâ€™ve written the next iconic rock riff anthem? Use the crunch channel! The tone has a surprising width and clarity. It won't get all flubby and turn your tone into mud. Vintage Makes your amp sound overloaded with a big bottom end, yet retains note separation on the higher strings. Things are about to get fuzzy. Fuzz 1 & 2 Inspired by mainstay fuzz pedal of the 60s garage rock. The original had a depth knob that really mixed two fuzz circuits and sometimes sounded like a broken octave effect.
